summary:
Lakshadweep stands under India's national framework. As a union territory without a full legislature, it has no separate trans statute: legal recognition, policing practice and identity-document rules that reach a visitor or resident are set by the central government. No Lakshadweep-specific recognition policy, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file.

Recognition narrowed in March 2026. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill passed both houses of Parliament and, as of the source dates, awaited presidential assent; Human Rights Watch, writing on 26 March 2026, called it a major reversal of the 2014 rights framework and urged the president not to sign it. The bill amends the 2019 law by removing the right to self-identification affirmed by the Supreme Court's 2014 third-gender ruling, narrowing the statutory definition of a transgender person, and mandating medical certification for identity recognition.

Legal recognition is now limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. The government argues the narrower definition improves delivery of welfare schemes; critics warn it excludes trans men, trans women, non-binary and gender-fluid people, and describe mandatory medical certification as an attack on privacy and dignity. The activist Akkai Padmashali characterises the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which the Supreme Court has read to cover gender identity; the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical examination by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities.
tangentialFactors:
Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Bans on conversion therapy from the Madras High Court's 2021 judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level rather than by the union territory. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Lakshadweep has no equivalent board on file, so a visitor to the territory should not expect the state-level infrastructure available elsewhere in India.
localsOnly:
Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

Residents of Lakshadweep seeking welfare coordination, housing subsidies, pensions or surgery through a transgender welfare board have no territory-level body on file; the boards described above operate in Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha.
outOfScopeNotes:
Presidential assent to the March 2026 amendment was unresolved at the source dates: one account records approval by both houses awaiting assent, another records an appeal to the president not to sign. Whether the bill has since been assented to, and whether any challenge has been filed, is not sourced here.

No Lakshadweep-specific enforcement data, arrest series, checkpoint incident or recognition decision is on file, so the territory's practical position is inferred from the national framework rather than observed locally.

The divergence in police-conduct assessments is unresolved: the United Kingdom's December 2025 note describes abuse as limited and non-systemic, while the June 2024 victim interviews document abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. Neither source covers Lakshadweep's police.

Whether the amendment's medical-certification requirement applies to passport issuance in Lakshadweep, and how territory-level document offices will implement it, is not sourced. The scale of clandestine conversion-therapy networks is likewise not quantified in the inventory.
